replying_to: Replying to MCL-GAN: Generative Adversarial Networks with Multiple Specialized Discriminators
display_title: Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer Qjrq

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes using multiple discriminators in GANs in order to better learn the diverse modes of the data and guide the GAN’s generator towards them, and therefore mitigate the problem of mode collapse. The main novelty compared to other multi-discriminator GANs is in the use of Multiple Choice Learning, where only a confident subset of discriminators are used for guiding the generator on each given sample, to ensure that discriminators specialize. The proposed model is applied to two GANs (StyleGAN2 and DCGAN) in various tasks, and shows improvements compared to some baseline single-discriminator and previous multi-discriminator GANs.
content.main_review:
**Strength:**

The adaptation of Multiple Choice Learning for multi-discriminator GANs is novel, and the specifics of how to use MCL can potentially be useful for other applications of adversarial learning in general. The paper provides experiments on various tasks which provides a broad sense of how well the model works. The organization is good and easy to follow for the most part.


**Concerns and Questions:**

1- The advantage of using MCL is not well motivated, the paper’s motivation goes only so far as this one sentence: “Note that all the existing approaches learn the multiple discriminators independently and they may have strong correlations, which may not be appropriate for diversifying the generated samples.” The “may have” and “may not” are not good motivations/justifications for the need of MCL. The toy example of section 5.1 would be a good place to highlight the shortcomings (e.g. the suggested correlations) in previous multi-discriminator GANs, but this experiment only compares with a single-discriminator baseline.

2- Another major concern is lack of comparison to the-state-of-the-art on the datasets used in the paper, namely small diverse datasets such as CIFAR-10. A recent finding is that the issue of mode collapse, which this paper is trying to address, could be the result of the discriminator overfitting to the limited training data, and consequently discriminator augmentations have been proposed as an effective solution [1]. This paper does not cite or compare with such works. In particular, StyleGAN2-ADA [1] is the current state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10 and several other small datasets, and given that the reported performance of that work far exceeds the numbers in this paper (see Figure 11a of [1]), it is unclear whether the proposed MCL-GAN is an orthogonal improvement to data discriminator augmentation, or will its effect fade when using the augmentations. I noticed that in Appendix I.2, the paper mentions using StyleGAN2-ADA repo but without its augmentation, which is the main contribution of that model, so why wasn't augmentation used?

3- While the paper provides experiments over various tasks (which is great), it is lacking in terms of systematic comparison to other multi-discriminator GANs, which in my opinion is much more important given that a myriad of such models have been proposed and it is crucial to highlight the advantages of this particular new model with respect to them. Specifically, I’d like to know why some GANs are dropped from some experiments (for example Table 3 and Figure 3 only compare with one multi-discriminator baseline).

4- A central claim in the paper is that the proposed MCL helps discriminators specialize and this will help improve multi-discriminator GANs’ performance. However, looking at Figure 4 in Appendix A, we see several discriminators (e.g. orange colored) cover multiple modes. Similarly in Figure 10 (k=1), several discriminators (e.g. mid to last rows) cover multiple modes. So the improvements cannot necessarily be the result of better specializations. Moreover, in Appendix F.3, the paper confirms that the use of L1 loss, which is proposed to ensure better specialization, is minimal on the performance metrics, placing more doubts on the main claim that more specialized discriminators results in less mode collapse (better performance). All these nuances, which seem contrary to the main premise of the paper, are absent from the main paper, and therefore could result in misleading conclusions for the reader.

5- The loss functions in Eq. 3,4,5 are inconsistent with how the GAN optimization is commonly carried out to avoid vanishing gradients. To elaborate, the discriminator objective is commonly written as log(D(x)) over real samples and log(1-D(x)) over fake samples, and this ensures that incorrectly classified samples receive large gradients (i.e. real samples with small D(x), and fake samples with large D(x)). However, the way Eq. 3,4 is written, namely log(1-D(x)) for real samples and log(D(x)) for fake samples, gradients will only be large on samples that are already correctly classified (i.e. real samples with large D(x) and fake samples with small D(x)). Same goes for Eq. 5. Is this just a notational error, or is this a deliberate choice and is used in implementation? If so, why?

[1] Karras, Tero, et al. "Training generative adversarial networks with limited data." NeurIPS 2020 (2020).
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern is whether this proposed model is in fact effective when combined with the current state-of-the-art discriminator augmentation GANs, particularly because these models already do a very good job of capturing variations in all the modes, and solve the mode collapse issue to a great extent (given that the paper already uses the StyleGAN2-ADA repo, it is not clear to me why the authors decided not to compare with StyleGAN2-ADA). The usefulness of the proposed model heavily relies on the aforementioned concern, and unless it is clarified, I cannot recommend this paper for acceptance. An additional concern is the paper's claim that MCL-GAN achieves better performance due to better specialization among discriminators, which is not consistent with some of the findings, as pointed out in the main review.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer Qjrq

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Please read our answers and let us know if you have any further issues or questions.

1. To clarify the mentioned sentence, the distribution over the data of each discriminator has higher correlations than specialized ones on the mutually exclusive subsets. The previous approaches are not explicitly designed to specialize the characteristics of each discriminator since the dataset is entirely shared. In this sense, comparison to GMAN justifies the benefits of specialized models. 

2. We used StyleGAN2 and the experimental setup used in Inclusive GAN [2] in order to make a fair comparison. In [2], they compare the results with other GAN methods which are proposed to address the mode collapse issue based on the same StyleGAN2 backbone. For this reason, we used the repo of [1] without using discriminator augmentation, with an equivalent setting with StyleGAN2, isolating the effect of the augmentation technique. 

3. We choose GMAN to verify the effect of specialization of discriminators by MCL as it has the closest configuration to ours. We would like to emphasize that, instead of comparing other similar papers with multiple discriminators, we focus on the applicability and practicability of our method and compare with some other methods which attempted to address the mode collapse as in Table 2 and 3. In effect, the results of Inclusive GAN referred to in Table 3, showed better results than many other methods that were proposed to mitigate the mode collapse and improve the sample diversity including Dist-GAN, PacGAN, VAEGAN, VEEGAN, etc. Meanwhile, we additionally run Albuquerque et al. [3], which is one of the recent approaches that utilize multiple discriminators, on CIFAR-10 and observed that the result of our method are superior to [3] with much fewer memory requirements (only 42.6% compared to [3]). We added this result in Table 2 in the revised manuscript.

4. Regarding Figure 4 in Appendix A, the orange-colored samples are drawn from true data. Considering this, the results show that two (/one) discriminators cover each mode, exclusively in (a) (/(b)). \
Also in Figure 10 (k=1), the clusters share some digits across different rows but we claim this is reasonable results since we do not use any class labels or clustering algorithm during training. For example, the 6$^{th}$ and 8$^{th}$ rows share the same digits, mostly 4 and 7, but digits in the 8$^{th}$ row are more tilted than those in the 6$^{th}$. Although the separations are as clear as actual classes, the natural clustering made by our algorithm is fairly reliable based on the results in Table 7 in Appendix E. The model ‘Label’ in Table 7 uses our multi-discriminator framework and assigns a distinct class for each discriminator given that the number of discriminators is the same as the number of classes.  \
Regarding Appendix F.3 results, we clarify that $L_1$ loss is to help find an appropriate number of discriminators. From experiments, we observe that this number is decided at an early stage of training. $L_1$ loss does not necessarily lead to the optimal results but suggests that the number of activated discriminators is sufficient for decent performance given a dataset. These suggestions are also quite stable through different initializations and the number of discriminators (see Table 12 in Appendix G) thus reliable. 

5. We apologize for the confusing equations. We corrected the equation (3) and (4) in the form of the original GAN minimax objective. The implementation follows the original GAN objective for discriminators and the modified objective, i.e., $\min -E_{z \sim p_z}\log D(G(z))$ for generator updates. We also added these implementation details in Appendix I.2 of the revised manuscript. 

[1] Karras et al. Training generative adversarial networks with limited data. NeurIPS 2020.

[2] Yu et al. Inclusive gan: Improving data and minority coverage in generative models. ECCV 2020.

[3] Albuquerque et al. Multi-objective training of generative adversarial networks with multiple discriminators. ICML 2019.

replying_to: Replying to MCL-GAN: Generative Adversarial Networks with Multiple Specialized Discriminators
display_title: Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer bNGB

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work improves upon generative multi-adversarial networks (GMAN) by incorporating ideas inspired by multiple choice learning (MCL) to diversify the discriminators. By encouraging the discriminators to diversify and specialize in different modes of the data distribution, the authors hope to better avoid the problem of mode collapse for the generator. The number of modes in the data distribution is, in general, unknown, so they propose overpopulating the number of discriminator experts and then learning to rely on a smaller subset via L1-regularization. To reduce the overhead that naturally comes with training multiple discriminators, they propose sharing portions of the network across discriminators. Experiments on synthetic, text, and image data reporting precision, recall, FID, and other metrics support the efficacy of the approach.
content.main_review:
Strengths: At a high level, the idea of diversifying the discriminators in GMAN to better specialize in distinct modes of the data distribution is sensible. And leaning on past approaches like multiple choice learning to encourage this behavior is a good idea. The approach also attains performance competitive with or better than prior models in many settings.

Weaknesses:
1) The precise approach taken is unclear. In particular, how are $v_{i,m}$ and $u_{j,m}$ set? These seem central to the training protocol. I understand the concepts from section 3 on multiple choice learning and the role of these variables, but I never saw a formula or learning rule provided for these variables. For example, if $v_{i,m} = 1$ iff $| \\{ p | D_m(x_i) < D_p(x_i) \\} | < k$, i.e., $D_m$ outputs one of the k-largest values, then this should be stated explicitly somewhere. Note this also implies that $v_{i,m}$ is a function of $D$ and a function of $D$'s parameters. When backprop'ing through the loss functions in equation (10), are these differentiated?
2) Given my confusion around $v_{i,m}$ and $u_{j,m}$, I was also confused how the balance losses affect the selection of experts. I understood from your discussion that equation (8) was introduced to encourage the discriminators to be similarly confident about samples in each minibatch to avoid pathologies early in training. However, I could not connect this with $v_{i,m}$ for a deeper understanding.
3) The losses used to train the discriminator and generator are not standard. The original GAN minimax objective is $V(G,D) = E_{x \sim p(x)} \log(D(x)) + E_{z \sim p(z)} \log(1-D(G(z)))$ where the generator minimizes V and the discriminator maximizes V (minimizes -V). To improve training speed, Goodfellow suggested replacing the second term in the generator's objective with $-E_{z \sim p(z)} \log(D(G(z)))$. In contrast, in your equation (3), the discriminator's loss is of the form $\log(1-D(x))$ which does not match any form of the standard objective I just repeated. I was expecting to see the discriminator minimize $-\log(D(x))$. Likewise, equation (4) has the discriminator additionally minimize $\log(D(G(z))$. Normally, I would expect to see minimizing $-\log(1-D(G(z)))$. To be clear, these objectives aren't entirely wrong, they are just not what are normally reported and no reason was give for this deviation from the norm.
4) Equation (6) seems to exist to discourage an expert on data mode X from also being an expert on data mode Y. Is that correct? This seems sensible for training the expert discriminators, but the rationale for a similar objective for the generator in equation (7) was not clear to me. Can you explain why you include equation (7)?
5) The comparison to GMAN is not clear. Note that in GMAN, the authors differentiate the discriminators by initializing them with different architectures. They give each discriminator a different dropout rate and vary the number of filters in the layers. They also feed each discriminator a different slice of the minibatch from the data. Did you do this as well? I would suggest pointing out in the text that GMAN differentiates discriminators through their architecture while you attempt to differentiate discriminators through which data you train them on. Also, GMAN introduces several variants. It explores using an arithmetic mean, harmonic mean, etc to aggregate the discriminators. It also introduces an automated way of adjusting the temperature of the softmax aggregator. Please specify these details in the paper.
6) One piece of literature worth including in your review in section 2.1 is PacGAN: The Power of Two Samples in Generative Adversarial Networks --- (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10168460).
7) Please spend a few sentences explaining the metrics NDB/JSD and LPIPS. Also, does "+MCL+MS" refer to MSGAN with your additional losses added?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I like the idea of diversifying the discriminators in GMAN to be experts on separate modes of the data and using MCL or other old techniques to accomplish this. But I felt like the approach was not described clearly which makes it difficult to assess. I also was unclear on which version of GMAN was being compared against. The exposition needs work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer bNGB

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
We appreciate your taking the time to provide us with valuable feedback. We respond to each of the questions and suggestions as follows.

1. The flag variables, $v_{i,m}$ and $u_{j,m}$, are equal to 1 if the score of $D_m$ is one of the k-largest values (as the reviewer understood). We termed the model with k-highest scores as experts at the beginning of Section 4.1. These variables are not included in the backpropagation since their role is to express that only subset of discriminators are updated for each sample. The real data are clustered naturally by the selection rule of MCL (k-max) rather than backpropagation which makes our method computationally efficient.

2. Regarding the connection between the balance loss and $v_{i,m}$, the balance loss avoids the vector 
$\mathbf{\hat{q}}=\frac{1}{kN_d}\sum_{i=1}^{N_d}[v_{i,0}, …, v_{i,M}] $ being too sparse. If $\mathbf{\hat{q}}$ is a one-hot vector, the training essentially becomes a single discriminator case. This does not particularly harm the original GAN performance but is not desirable results for using multi-discriminators. By adopting the soft-maxed output vectors in equation (8), which is differentiable, instead of $\mathbf{\hat{q}}$, it is possible to enforce the frequencies of highest scores to be distributed through discriminators.  

3. We apologize for the confusing equations. We corrected the equation (3) and (4) in the form of the original GAN minimax objective. The implementation follows the original GAN objective for discriminators and the modified objective, i.e., $\min -E_{z \sim p_z}\log D(G(z))$ for generator updates. We also added these implementation details in Appendix I.2 of the revised manuscript. 

4. Equation (7) encourages the generated samples to be regarded as real samples with respect to the discriminators. If expert training (equation (5)) pulls the sample toward the closest subset of real data, (7) ensures the lowered confidence of the models that are expert on the other subsets. 

5. For differentiating discriminators of GMAN, we used different dropout rates in [0.4, 0.6] for each discriminator while using the same architectures as DCGAN (and ours). Also, we used the split of mini-batches for the input of discriminators. Among several variants of GMAN, we choose three versions that use the arithmetic mean of softmax, i.e., GMAN-1, GMAN-0 and GMAN*, which are reported as the best models on different datasets in the literature. We choose the best scores among them to compare with our method. We updated the details of the GMAN setting in Appendix I.2 of the revised manuscript.

6. We added the recommended literature in Section 2.1 of the revised version. 

7. We added a brief explanation of the metrics, NDB/JSD and LPIPS in Appendix J.1 of the revised version. “+MCL+MS” refers to MSGAN (mode-seeking regularization term) is applied on top of the loss of our method.

display_title: Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer pRtx

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a technique to train GANs with multiple discriminators inspired from Multiple Choice Learning (MCL). This hasn’t been done to date in my knowledge. The idea is to make the discriminators specialize on a subset of the data via clever design of the loss function.
content.main_review:
There are several things I like about the paper:
1. The approach seems to be novel especially the part about balancing discriminator updates and non-expert training.
2. A new technique (to my knowledge) in order to adjust the number of discriminators used during training on the fly.
3. Good breadth of ablation studies (in the appendix)  

Here are some of my thoughts/criticisms:
1. Unclear why there is no comparison with Neyshabur et al. and Albuquerque et al. and other similar papers. These seem like direct competitors to the proposed method (multiple discriminators) and are more recent than GMAN (which is used as a baseline). I think this is the biggest drawback of the paper as it stands. There is no way at the moment to conclude how good the performance actually is wrt prior work.
2. Training with multiple discriminators would increase model parameters. A fair comparison would require baselines which account for this.
3. Datasets which are used in the paper are small. It is hard to tell whether the proposed technique works only in small settings (both in terms of image dimension and diversity) vs much more diverse settings like ImageNet (or its subsets). As it stands, the improvements in diversity seem to be marginal. 

Formatting/Typos:
There are several minor grammatical mistakes (too many to list). I hope the authors re-read the manuscript and correct them. Some examples:
1. Section 4.1 “encourage the generator finds the closest mode” should be “encourage the generator to find the closest mode” 
2. Section 4.3 “This adjustment helps stable training and ” should be “This adjustment helps stablize training and ”
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the lack of a fair evaluation and writing issues lead me to not recommend publication.

replying_to: Replying to MCL-GAN: Generative Adversarial Networks with Multiple Specialized Discriminators
display_title: Official Review of Paper513 by Reviewer h6xM

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors use multiple choice learning to improve mode diversity in GAN training. In particular, the authors propose using a mixture of expert discriminators, each one focusing on a subset of dataset, which are in turn used to train the generator network. With several balancing terms in the objective, each discriminator is made to focus on subset of samples and the generator model is trained to fool every discriminator. Results show that using multiple discriminators improve sample quality and mode coverage.
content.main_review: While the authors demonstrate the use of multiple discriminators in GAN training, I have these major issues: (1) The idea is similar to GMAN and I feel authors have not done a good job in studying the differences between the approaches and justifying why (and what specific component) their approach is better than GMAN, and (2) With the provided experimental results, I am not very convinced the need for using multiple discriminators in the first place, (3) The approach seems to involve a lot of balancing terms which would need careful tuning to prevent some denegrate solutions.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea of the paper is very similar to GMAN where the multiple discriminator setup is used. The authors need to talk about the differences more clearly. In my opinion, both GMAN and the current paper uses max-critic to train the generator. As the authors mentioned in last paragraph of page 1, the only difference lies in the method of ensembling. The authors should study the effect of this component in more depth since this is the only point of difference in both approaches.

More specifically, have the authors used the same architectures and tricks for comparing GAN training between GMAN and their approach, with the only point of difference being the ensembling approach? This experiment is needed to study the effect of ensemling.

In the approach, it is not clear how the variables u’s and v’s are optimized. Do we assign one vector for each sample and  optimize them? If so, the number of optimization variables increases with number of samples which may be problematic for large datasets. If not, then how are they optimized?

The approach seems to involve a lot of balancing terms which are really needed to ensure that all discriminators are utilized and each one focuses on a distinct subset of samples. This needs careful tuning which might not be too desirable.

In page 5, “for each example since the discriminator with the highest score is guaranteed to be chosen as an expert. “ Is this guaranteed? From the formulation, the decision to choose the expert relies on the variable v and u. Its not clear how v and u are optimized?

There are some papers that use multiple generators and one discriminator? The point being each generator focusses on one subset of the data. This makes sense. How does this compare with multi-discriminator setup used in the paper? Which one is better - what are the tradeoffs? Can multi-generator multi-discriminator setup be used?

If the discriminator is complex enough, do we need multiple discriminators? With the success of deep models like StyleGAN and BigGAN, the complexity of discriminators keep increasing drastically. This begs the question “what benefit do we really gain by using multiple discriminators?”

From the experiments, the authors show that their approach is beneficial. But, the FID scores of SOTA models on CIFAR and CelebA have gone much lower than what has been reported here (For example, BigGAN has a FID of 14.73 in CIFAR). With this in mind, I am not sure about the importance of these results reported here.

How exactly are the precision  and recall metrics calculated here?

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. We hope to have active discussions to clarify all the issues and misunderstandings. Please read our answers and let us know if you have any further issues or questions.

**Differences from GMAN**

The main difference between our method and GMAN is the specialization of discriminators. We use the max-criterion to train the generator but also to train the discriminators to be specialized on the subset of the real dataset. While discriminators of GMAN do not share the parameters, ours share the parameters except for the last layer, which in turn, makes our algorithm more computationally efficient (see Appendix H). Also, we introduce some loss terms, (e.g., balance loss and non-expert training loss) to facilitate our training and discuss the effect of these components in Appendix F. Besides, GMAN reports that max-critic does not work well in practice and better ensemble results are obtained from the soft-critic. 

**Comparison setting**

We made the comparison to GMAN based on the same DCGAN architecture. We used the official code of GMAN to test their variants and choose the best score to report. We have updated the manuscript with detailed settings of GMAN in Appendix I.2.

**Decisions on u and v variables**

The variables $u_{i,m}$ and $v_{j,m}$ are flag variables that are decided by the discriminators’ scores in analogy to those in the original MCL algorithm. To be precise, the variables are assigned to 1 for the best scores of discriminators for each sample and to 0 for the others. Thus, the method is free from the optimization of variables and scalability issues. 

**Ablations on balance losses**

The performance is not critically sensitive to the coefficient of the balance losses and surpasses a single discriminator GAN with a large margin throughout the wide range of the choice of the coefficient. We provide the ablation studies on balance loss terms in Appendix F.2. 

**Multiple generators**

Naive approaches of GAN with MCL would employ multiple generators for the diversity in outputs instead of using multiple discriminators, which leads to the increase of inference cost. However, the proposed work does not change the network architecture of a generator or generation process (e.g., selection rules among samples). Besides, the method does not have any restrictions on extending to multi-generator multi-discriminator setup. For instance, it is plausible to design a multi-generator with the same number of discriminators and update the generator $G_i$ to be the expert on the subset corresponding to the discriminator $D_i$. 

**Benefits on complex models**

The experiments on the SytleGAN2 architecture and conditioned image generation tasks show that our method is also effective with complex discriminators. Since the discriminators of MCL-GAN share all layers except the last one, the increment of model parameters becomes smaller for deeper models, which is promising.

**Meaning of results in Table 1&2**

We primarily focus on the proof of our concept on several GAN losses based on the basic architecture, i.e., DCGAN, which would be more helpful to understand the behavior of the proposed method than complex and large models. The FID scores on CIFAR (in Table 2) show that our method improves the baseline with great margin but also other methods on the same architecture and underlying GAN loss. For example, the performance of our method which conducts unconditional generation is better than the MSGAN results which utilize the class labels on the generation.

**Evaluation method of precision/recall**

We measure the precision and recall based on the official code of Precision Recall Distribution (PRD) [1]. Please refer to Appendix J.1 for the details.

[1] Mehdi S. M. Sajjadi et al. Assessing Generative Models via Precision and Recall. NeurIPS 2018.
